summary: This experimental memo proposes short-term solutions for keeping and distributing routing information for X.400 message handling, and shows how messages can travel over different networks using multi-stack relays.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1465 defines documents that describe X.400 mail domains, relay servers, contact people and supported network connections. Message transfer agents use the documents to choose a relay and retry another route when a connection fails.

subtitle: A V3 table format for coordinating X.400 mail routing across domains, relays and networks.

tldr.problem: X.400 message transfer agents need shared routing information when a community spans domains and network stacks. They also need a way to reach a domain when its MTA does not share the same network technology.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines Community, Relay-MTA, Domain and Person documents. Relay descriptions list the stacks and addresses they support; domain entries identify responsible relays and assign priorities.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1465 is Experimental. It proposes a short-term, table-based coordination method that the RFC describes as a bridge toward directory-based routing.

today: RFC 1465 is Experimental. It defines a V3 document format and coordination procedures for static routing in X.400 MHS communities.

sections.title: Why X.400 Routing Needs Coordination
sections.content:
The RFC addresses two problems for X.400 Message Handling Systems: where to route new addresses and how to connect to a domain that uses a different underlying technology. X.400 MTAs can use different network and transport stacks, and the RFC says communication requires a common stack and a common network.

Its proposed table format and coordination procedures are intended as a short-term solution while an X.500 directory service is not yet available to store routing information. The document calls this its third version of the table format.
sections.plainLanguage: X.400 mail servers may use different network technologies and need shared routing information. This RFC sets out a document-based method for sharing that information.

sections.title: Four Documents Describe the Community
sections.content:
A Community document identifies the community, its coordination contact, file server, and mandatory and optional network services. A Relay-MTA document describes one relay's supported stacks, addresses and connection details. A Domain document identifies address subtrees and the relays that serve them. A Person document holds administrator contact information.

Documents use a defined V3 text format. Communities maintain and distribute them through a coordination point, which also helps test new relays and assists new domains.
sections.plainLanguage: The community document describes the group. The other documents describe its relays, mail domains and contacts, so people and tools can share routing details.

sections.title: Choosing and Retrying a Relay
sections.content:
An MTA finds the Domain entry that matches a recipient address, then keeps relays that share a supported service type with itself. It selects the highest-priority relay; a lower priority number means higher priority. If a connection fails, it tries other service types and then other suitable relays according to their priorities.

Primary relays must connect to all other primary relays that share a stack. A secondary relay must connect to at least one primary relay. A domain may also rely on relays operated by other MHS services.
sections.plainLanguage: An MTA checks which relays serve a recipient's domain and chooses one it can reach. If that connection fails, it can try another service type or a lower-priority relay.

sections.title: Keeping Routing Documents Current
sections.content:
Each community identifies a coordination point and decides how much support it will provide. Required activities include testing new relay MTAs, helping domains prepare documents, announcing updates unless distribution is automatic, and making the documents available on a file server reachable by email.

The RFC notes that a community with about 60 relay MTAs may be manageable with automated configuration tools. It also identifies larger-scale coordination and the transition to X.500-based routing as open issues.
sections.plainLanguage: A coordination point keeps routing documents available and helps new participants join. The RFC notes that maintaining many relays requires tools and ongoing coordination.
